1:
Why the wilderness at all is answered first by the fathers. Theophylact reads the sequence as a warning: Christ is tempted after his baptism, to show us that temptations await us after ours. Ambrose gives three reasons — to provoke the devil, since if the one had not contended the other had not conquered; in a mystery, to bring back the Adam cast out of Paradise into the wilderness; and by way of example, to show how the devil envies us whenever we strive after better things. Cyril of Alexandria puts it as substitution: he took the form of a slave and set himself as an avenger in our stead against the serpent, that we might conquer in him where of old we fell in Adam. Henry makes the point from the close of the previous chapter — that Jesus was the Son of Adam bespeaks him the seed of the woman, so that at the beginning of the war he conquers the conqueror.

Whether the forty days were themselves tempted divides them. Basil says the Lord remained forty days untempted, since the devil knew that he fasted and yet did not hunger, and so dared not approach him; hunger came at the end and, wherever hunger is, weakness is, so the tempter came then. Barnes says the same, that the recorded temptations did not take place until the forty days were finished. Gill reports the versions that produce the division — the Vulgate, Syriac, Persic and Ethiopic attach the forty days to the previous sentence — but keeps the received reading, and suggests that Satan may have tempted him invisibly, by internal suggestion, before appearing openly. Basil adds what the hunger means: not to suffer hunger is above the nature of man, and he took the feeling upon himself, not forced by necessity but provoking the devil to the conflict.

How he was brought there is disputed by the moderns. Clarke sets the three verbs side by side — Luke's carried about, Matthew's brought up, Mark's driveth forth — and insists that all three attribute the leading to the Holy Ghost and not to Satan, so that the forty days were forty days of being sustained; it matters little, he says, how many days a man is assaulted while he is carried about by the Spirit. Robertson makes the verb a continuous imperfect and notes that Luke names the Spirit twice in one sentence; he quotes Plummer that the temptation was to use supernatural power for his own interests without regard to the Father's will, and observes that this narrative, absent from Mark, is a specimen of the earliest document about Christ and could have come only from Christ himself. Lightfoot goes further than anyone: he supposes Christ was literally caught up into the air by the Spirit, as Philip was and as was supposed of Elijah, and adds that the devil might have snatched him up in the same way, pretending to be the Holy Ghost and on that pretence demanding worship. He also notes that Luke's order differs from Matthew's, the pinnacle standing second there and third here, and that Moses fasted forty days three times where once sufficed for Christ. Wesley locates the desert, some supposing it in Judea and others the great waste of Horeb where Israel was tried forty years.

On the first temptation the notes are short. Ellicott observes that Luke's singular this stone is more vivid than Matthew's plural, and Robertson guesses at a particular round stone shaped like a loaf, recalling the crystallised stones on Carmel that are called Elijah's melons. Cyril of Jerusalem, reached here only by the phrase about fulness of the Spirit, follows it forward instead to the seven deacons chosen full of the Holy Ghost and to Stephen, whose face in the council was as an angel's.
5:
How the kingdoms were shown gets three incompatible answers. Theophylact reports that some say the devil presented them in imagination, and states his own view against them: he brought them before Christ in visible form. Robertson takes the opposite line, calling the panorama mental, a feat of the imagination, while insisting this in no way discredits an actual visible appearance of Satan. Ellicott offers a third, that the compression of an almost endless succession of images into the consciousness of a moment is characteristic of the soul in ecstasy or vision. On the moment itself Robertson notes that Luke's word means a point or prick, used nowhere else in the New Testament and answering to our tick of the clock; Lightfoot goes to the rabbis and reports, dryly, that they make a moment the fifty-eight thousand eight hundred and eighty-eighth part of an hour. Ellicott adds that Luke's word for the world is the one taken as co-extensive with the Roman empire.

The order of the temptations is the standing problem, and the three who raise it answer it differently. Gill says Luke makes this the second where Matthew makes it the third, and that Matthew's is the true order, which Luke neglects without contradicting — Luke relating facts without attending to sequence, while Matthew marks it with then and again and closes with the devil leaving him. Clarke agrees that this temptation stands last in Matthew and that it is unreasonable to suppose another followed it, so that Luke gives the particulars but not the sequence. Robertson refuses to choose and characterises both: Luke's order is geographical — wilderness, mountain, Jerusalem — and Matthew's climactic — hunger, nervous dread, ambition — though Luke's has a climax of its own, sense, man, God; and there is no way to tell the actual order.

The devil's claim to have received the kingdoms divides them sharply. Ellicott says the notion that any such sovereignty was ever delegated to the tempter has no foundation in Scripture, which declares the earth the Lord's, so the claim was a lying boast resting on the permitted predominance of evil. Robertson observes the opposite fact about the text, that Satan claims possession of world power and Jesus does not deny it, and suggests it may be owing to man's sin and God's permission, Jesus himself calling Satan the ruler of this world. Wesley answers the claim rather than analysing it — not so, Satan; it is God who putteth down one and setteth up another, though Satan by permission may occasion great revolutions. Cyril of Jerusalem answers it with the words it parodies: riches and gold are not the devil's, since God says the gold is his and the silver is his and he gives it to whom he will; and money may become a door of the kingdom when it feeds the hungry and clothes the naked.

On what was being asked for, the notes converge. Ambrose distinguishes the thing from its use: all power is from God, and the lust of power from the evil one, power itself not being evil but he who uses it evilly; and he presses the irony that to rule others a man must first be their servant, prostrating himself to be rewarded with honours. Gill sets the fallen angel against the good one, who refuses worship and directs men to God, whereas this one sought worship from the Son of God himself — the very thing he first aspired to and fell by. Robertson reduces the demand to its smallest form, just to bow the knee once in Satan's presence, and states what acceptance would have made of him: the agent of Satan in ruling the world by bargain and graft, instead of the Son of God ruling by conquest over him. He adds that Luke omits the dismissal Matthew records, having a third temptation still to narrate.
9:
Ambrose names the third weapon and explains why the pinnacle suits it. The weapon is boasting, which always causes the offender to fall, since those who love to boast of the glory of their virtue come down from the vantage ground of their own good deeds; and the devil's language is precisely language that seeks to cast the soul down from that height. In doing so, Ambrose says, he shows at once his weakness and his malice, for he can injure no one who does not first cast himself down — a man who forsakes heavenly things for earthly rushes willingly down a self-sought precipice. He adds the turn that follows: as soon as the devil perceived his dart blunted, he who had subdued all men to his own power began to think he had to deal with more than man. Origen puts the same moment from the other side, that Christ followed as a wrestler gladly setting out to meet the temptation, as if to say, lead me where you will and you will find me the stronger in everything.

Who exactly was being tempted is then pressed. Athanasius observes that the devil did not enter into a contest with God, for he did not dare, which is why he said if thou art the Son of God; his contest was with the man he had once had power to deceive. He adds that the enemy came to Christ as to a man but, not finding in him the marks of his ancient seed, departed. Ambrose reads the departure the same way, that the devil is not obstinate in the field but gives way to true virtue, and that if he does not cease to hate he yet dreads to advance, so escaping a more frequent defeat; and that the season for which he left was the interval before he came again not to tempt but to fight openly. Maximus supplies what filled that interval, that the devil, having failed to make Christ prefer the world to the love of God, afterwards stirred up Gentiles and Pharisees to lay traps for him, so that he might be brought to hate them and appear the false advocate of love — and that the Lord, from the love he bore them, went on exhorting, reproving and showing mercy.

The disagreement over the order of the temptations reappears, and the answers get shorter. Augustine grants that Matthew relates the whole in a similar manner but not in the same order, says it is uncertain which came first, and holds that it matters little which, provided it is clear that they all took place. Maximus offers a reason for the variation rather than a decision, that vain-glory and covetousness give birth in turn to one another, so that either may stand first.

On the quotation the moderns are exact. Robertson observes that Satan does not misquote the psalm but misapplies it, making it mean a presumptuous reliance on God, and notes that Luke adds a clause about guarding that Matthew's version of the quotation lacks. Gill reports the older observation, which he credits to Jerome, that Satan in citing the text has dropped the middle clause. Gill also brings Christ to the place, from the wilderness to the holy city and the pinnacle of the temple, and suggests that here too he may have been brought through the air; Robertson admits that it is not easy to determine precisely what the wing of the temple was.
12:
Robertson notes that Luke writes it is said where Matthew writes it is written, and that each of the three answers is drawn from Deuteronomy and quoted from the Greek version; he adds Plummer's summary of what the answer means, that testing God is not trusting God.

What all the temptation covers is then the question. Gill takes it as widely as it will go — not the last only but all the rest, inward or outward, visible or invisible, during the fast or after it — and gathers the versions, the Syriac reading all his temptations, the Ethiopic adding that the devil did it with all his power, the Persic that he profited nothing. Ellicott would render it had completed every kind of temptation, and explains why the number is three: each trial was typical, and together they made up the cycle of those to which our Lord's human nature was then open. Robertson says the same in his own terms, that the three exhaust the avenues of approach — the appetites, the nerves, the ambitions — so that he was in all points tempted as we are, and quotes Plummer that the enemy tried all his weapons and was at all points defeated; but he also holds that the devil probably tempted him throughout the forty days and that the three stand for all, which is Gill's position and not Ellicott's.

The season for which the devil left is identified the same way by five voices, who differ only over the mechanism. Wesley gives the shortest answer, the garden of Gethsemane. Ellicott sets it at the close of the great work, the hour of the power of darkness, when the prince of this world came again and, trying now the power of suffering where he had before tried the allurement of the world, was foiled in the second as in the first. Robertson takes the phrase to mean until a good opportunity should return, infers that the devil came back from time to time, and holds that the assault in Gethsemane was the severer, aimed at making him draw back from the cross where this one had aimed at tripping him at the start. Lightfoot describes the change of method rather than the moment: the devil had found by experience how vain it was to tempt by suggestion, and watched for an opportunity of trying his arts another way, which he took at last both in his own person and through his instruments — and when that season drew near we read of Satan entering into Judas. Barnes draws the pastoral conclusion instead, that no later temptations are recorded though the Saviour was certainly subject to them, that Satan probably did much to excite the Pharisees and the rulers against him, and that as God delivered him out of all of them he will make a way of escape for everyone who is tempted.
14:
What was added when Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit is the first question, and the two Greek fathers answer it in opposite directions. Origen says that power was added to him once the tempter was overcome — adding at once the qualification, as far as regards the manifestation of it. Cyril denies any addition at all: Christ performed miracles not from an external power, nor from an acquired grace of the Spirit as other saints do, but as being by nature the Son of God and partaking of everything that is the Father's, so that he exercises as his own the grace that is of the Spirit. Ellicott describes the change in terms close to Origen's qualification — a new phase of the life of the Son of Man, as striking as the change that passed over the Apostles at Pentecost, when powers of thought and utterance before latent were developed. Wesley says only that he was more abundantly strengthened after his conflict, and Gill that the Spirit that led him out and conquered is the Spirit in which he now enters his ministry, comparing a Targum's phrase about being filled with the spirit of prophecy.

Clarke draws the moral rather than the doctrine: whoever by grace overcomes temptation is the better for it, and it is among the wonders of grace that the very things designed for our ruin are made the instruments of our greatest good, so that Satan is duped by his own proceedings. Henry notices instead where the ministry began — a remote part of the country, far from Jerusalem, which he counts part of the humiliation — and that Christ did not wait for a call from men, having light and life in himself.

Robertson supplies the frame. Luke does not fill the gap between the wilderness and Galilee but follows Mark's outline, and it is John alone who tells of the intervening year; these two verses give three marks of the Galilean ministry — the power of the Spirit, the spread of his fame, the use of the synagogues. He notes that the word for power is the one our dynamite comes from, and that the word for fame is built on the verb to say, so that what is described is talk running rapidly. Ellicott makes the same point about the sequence, reminding the reader that several chapters of John belong between the temptation and this beginning.

On the reception the notes divide between explanation and warning. Calvin says Luke records it expressly to inform us that from the very commencement a divine power shone in Christ, compelling even those who cherished a malignant spirit of contradiction to join in admiring him. Robertson takes it as a description of habit — the synagogues stood open before Pharisaic hostility was roused, and even the rabbis had not yet learned how to ridicule and oppose him. Barnes says simply that all were pleased with his instructions and admired his wisdom. Ellicott calls it the bright dawn of the day of work, and warns that when the preaching began to demand faith and obedience it roused the opposition that follows; Wesley makes the same point in his own idiom, that God usually gives strong cordials after strong temptations, but that neither their approbation nor the calm lasted long. Clarke turns the open synagogue into a rebuke of his own time: not even the persecuting Jews ever hindered Christ or his disciples from preaching in their synagogues, and he asks whether Jesus or his apostles would be allowed to preach in one church in a thousand where Christianity is established by law, unless they conformed and taught to the taste of the managers.
16:
The custom of attending draws the same pastoral rule from two commentators. Barnes infers from Christ's regular presence that it is better to attend a place of worship not entirely pure, where the doctrine is not what we would wish, than not to attend at all; Clarke says the other parts of the Jewish worship were very corrupt but this was the best then in the land, and that a man who cannot get such worship as he likes should frequent such as he can — better the most indifferent than staying at home. Lightfoot supplies the procedure from the rabbis: they read standing, and it was unlawful even to lean, one teacher rebuking a man who leaned against a pillar. Wesley states it compactly, that the custom was to read standing but preach sitting, and Robertson gives the order of service — the attendant taking a roll from the ark, seven readers from the law, then a prophetic reading with a discourse, the part Jesus took.

Whether the passage was appointed or chosen divides them three ways. Ellicott infers from the handing of the roll that it held the lesson for the day, and notes that in the modern Jewish calendar this chapter is the second lesson for the day of Atonement. Clarke agrees, and has Jesus unrolling the manuscript until he came to it. Calvin will not have it: Christ deliberately selected the passage, and though some think it was presented to him by God, a liberty of choice was allowed him and he took this one by his own judgement. Wesley goes another way, that he found it, opening upon it, by the particular providence of God. On the roll Lightfoot declines to say whether Isaiah came alone or bound with the other prophets, citing a rabbinic direction to frame all three divisions into one volume; Barnes says it would seem the books were kept separate, and Ellicott that here it is clear Isaiah formed a roll by itself. Both note that the text as read is not simply Isaiah: Ellicott that it follows the Greek version with a clause absent from the present Hebrew, Clarke that a second passage from another chapter is joined to the first.

The acceptable year is agreed to allude to the jubilee, and produces a rebuke of the fathers. Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and Calvin all make the connection, Calvin adding that the prophet anticipates the doubt of minds held in suspense by a long-delayed salvation, making the time of redemption depend on the good pleasure of God. Ellicott observes that a slavish literalism led some of the Fathers to infer from the word year that the ministry lasted twelve months, and Robertson names two early Alexandrian writers who argued it, adding that this is to turn figures into fact.

The sitting down is read against modern instinct. Ellicott says it suggests to us a falling back into obscurity, where to a Jew it implied the opposite, the chair by the reading-place being the rabbi's pulpit; Robertson takes it for the sign that he meant to speak. Calvin explains the fixed eyes by an astonishment God sent, which made them attentive and kept them from interrupting. Barnes and Ellicott agree that what stands here is only the substance or opening of the sermon, Ellicott adding what startled them: he had left them the son of the carpenter and returned claiming to be the Christ. Tertullian turns the name of the town against Marcion: the Christ of the Creator had to be called a Nazarene by prophecy, so Marcion's Christ should have avoided the Creator's localities altogether. Gill notes that the Spirit was given to Christ as man without measure; Cyril of Jerusalem follows the opening clause not into the sermon but into the Acts, where the Spirit speaks to Philip and separates Barnabas and Saul — living, calling, sending with authority.
22:
What the witness amounted to is disputed at once. Gill draws a fine line: they bore witness that he was right in applying the words to the Messiah, not that he was the Messiah, since they did not believe in him. Barnes takes the opposite, that they were struck because one they had long known now claimed to be the Christ and gave so much evidence of it. Calvin holds both halves together — they are compelled to acknowledge God speaking in Christ and yet refuse the honour, turning what should have glorified God into a ground of offence. Ellicott notes that the noun rendered grace is absent from Matthew and Mark, becomes prominent in the Acts, and is afterwards the characteristic word of two apostles; Wesley says a man of spiritual discernment finds in our Lord's discourses a sweetness not present in the same degree even in the apostles'; and Clarke complains that no evangelist reports the sermon, concluding that had it been necessary to salvation it would have been recorded.

Why no miracle was done there is answered four ways. Chrysostom says he refrained lest he provoke greater malice, setting his teaching before them instead, which was no less wonderful. Ambrose makes it a judgement on envy: the Lord withdraws his miracles from those jealous of his blessings in others, so that a country was deemed unworthy of its citizen's works which had been worthy of the conception of the Son of God. Cyril explains it by a common failing, that the best things are despised when they are always at a man's disposal, as a friend who is ever at hand does not meet the respect due to him. Calvin puts it as a withholding rather than an inability — men cannot bind God's hands, but he keeps back the benefit of his works from those unbelief has made unworthy — and Wesley says flatly that it is their unbelief.

Origen notices a difficulty in the sequence and turns it into allegory: as far as Luke's narrative goes no miracle has yet been done at Capernaum, so a mystery must lie concealed, Nazareth standing for the Jews and Capernaum for the Gentiles, the time coming when Israel will ask that what was shown to the whole world be shown to them. Basil allegorises the widow, every soul bereft of virtue learning, on receiving the divine word, to nourish it with the bread of virtue. Ellicott reads the two examples as a specimen of method — in what seemed a mere episode of Elijah's life Christ finds a truth implying the calling of the Gentiles — while Lightfoot explains their double offence, galling the hearers first by ranking them with an unworthy Israel and then by intimating that calling, than which nothing could be more grating in a Jewish ear. Clarke draws the general rule: God dispenses his benefits when, where and to whom he pleases, since justice depends on rules but beneficence is free.

The proverb and the chronology occupy the rest. Ellicott finds it interesting that the physician's proverb stands in the physician's Gospel, and wonders whether Luke heard it casually and tracked it to this history; Robertson notes that Luke alone reports it and that it recurs in two Greek tragedians and in Cicero. Barnes insists it implies no reflection on Christ's own condition. On the three years and six months the harmonies differ: Lightfoot allows that the number is often used allusively but sees no reason not to take it literally here, admitting the difficulty; Wesley reconciles it by counting the third year of the Kings narrative from the arrival at Sarepta, with a year at the brook before; Robertson calls it the popular Jewish way of speaking. Cyril of Jerusalem, reached by the formula of asseveration, uses it to introduce the ways of gaining eternal life rather than anything in the story.
28:
What exactly enraged them is given several ways. Cyril says they took him to be comparing himself with the prophets. Ellicott says they heard themselves spoken of as though there might be a faith in Zidon and in Syria that was not found in Israel, and of which they were altogether destitute. Robertson puts it bluntly: town pride was insulted and exploded, since the examples implied that Nazareth was no better than Capernaum and had no claim on unusual favours because he was reared there. Barnes lists five grounds, from their refusal of the evidence to their suspicion that they might be worse than Gentiles. Clarke states the inference more starkly and then concedes it: they gathered that the Gentiles were more precious in God's sight and his mercies chiefly reserved for them — which, he says, was pretty near the truth, as the event proved, the kingdom being taken from the Jews not because the Gentiles were better but because the privileges had been forfeited. Calvin observes what did not happen: instead of having their consciences stung to the quick and seeking a remedy by correcting their vices, they are only driven to madness. Wesley draws the moral rather than the doctrine — so changeable are the hearts of wicked men, and so unable are they to bear the close application of a discourse they had just admired.

The escape divides into a question about the person and a question about the law. Chrysostom finds both natures in it: to stand among men plotting against him and not be seized betokened the loftiness of his divinity, while his departure declared the mystery of the incarnation. Ambrose presses it as a matter of will — the bodily endurance was not necessary but voluntary, and when he wills he is taken and when he wills he escapes, for how could he be held by a few who was not held by a whole people. Bede gives three reasons why this could not be the moment: the hour of the Passion had not come, nor had he reached the place of it, which was not Nazareth but Jerusalem, nor was this the kind of death appointed, since it was prophesied that he should be crucified. Gill canvasses the mechanism — whether he passed so swiftly that they could not lay hold of him, or took another form, or made himself invisible, or held their eyes — and draws from it that when he did die he laid down his life freely, since he could have exerted the same power then.

Lightfoot asks by what authority or legal process the men of Nazareth could have done this at all. There was a court of three in the town, because there was a synagogue, but it had no power in capital matters, and he asks whether the licence allowed the zealots stretched so far. Barnes says flatly that they had no legal right to take life, least of all in this furious and irregular manner, and that the transaction confirms the character given elsewhere of the Galileans. Ellicott adds that casting from a height was not a recognised Jewish punishment as flinging from the Tarpeian rock was at Rome, though there is an instance of it improvised in a king's treatment of Edomite prisoners. Robertson calls the movement simply a lynching.

On the place itself the tradition is reported and then doubted. Barnes locates it at the Mount of Precipitation, still shown a short way south of the town; Clarke quotes a traveller's description of the climb through a narrow cleft to a great stone on the brink of a precipice, said to be the very spot. Ellicott says the hill now shown is about two miles from the city and can hardly be the place, and points instead to a cliff some forty feet high close to the town.
31:
Why he went to Capernaum is answered by motive and by fact. Ambrose says it was neither indignation at his treatment nor displeasure at their wickedness that moved him, but that, unmindful of his injuries, he softened this unbelieving people by teaching and healing in turn. Cyril adds the physician's figure: though he knew them hard of heart he visited them, as a good physician tries to heal the mortally sick, and taught them openly, having not spoken in secret. Gill notes the descent, Capernaum lying some sixteen miles off and Nazareth on a hill; Clarke and Wesley take him to have made Capernaum his home from this point; Ellicott observes that Luke supplies the reason for the removal where Matthew does not; and Robertson that Capernaum now becomes the headquarters, Luke here following Mark in the first miracle the two of them give.

Bede states the rule that a teacher's word has power when he performs what he teaches, and is despised when his actions belie it; Cyril observes that Christ intermingles mighty works with teaching, since those whose reason does not incline to knowledge are roused by miracles; and Ambrose finds significance in the day, healing beginning on the sabbath to show that he began anew where the old creation ceased and that the Son of God was not under the Law but above it. Henry takes the plainer lesson, that hearing the word preached is itself worship and proper sabbath work, and that there was weight in every word. Tertullian is arguing elsewhere: against Marcion's dating of the descent to Capernaum he presses the absurdity of a Christ coming down from his own heaven to the Creator's and thence to Galilee.

The unclean spirit draws the lexical notes. Lightfoot calls the phrase unusual and thinks it may point to the pythonic or necromantic spirit; Clarke remarks that the inspired writers never use the word in a good sense; Robertson says the combination is unique and counts its frequency against Matthew and Mark. Calvin reads the wording as meaning that the man was driven by the devil's impulse, Satan having seized his faculties so as to move and speak in him at pleasure. On the cry, Cyril explains its purpose from the later charge that Christ cast out devils by Beelzebub, the devils crying because they could not endure the divine presence; Chrysostom says the devil wished to disturb the order of things and rob the Apostles of their dignity; and Ambrose that it ought to shock nobody that a devil is the first in this book to speak the name of Jesus of Nazareth, since Christ did not receive that name from him. Wesley connects the confession with the wilderness: had the tempter known a little earlier that this was God over all, he would not have dared tell him that the power of the kingdoms was delivered to him — and this confession was either extorted by terror or designed to make the character suspected. Cyril of Jerusalem follows the exorcism into the Acts, where Philip drives out unclean spirits by the same power.

The moderns notice what Luke alone records. Robertson calls the interjection a diabolical screech, frequent in the Attic poets but rare in prose, the verb for silencing meaning to muzzle; on the throwing down he says Luke as a physician carefully records that the man took no hurt, a detail Mark lacks, and Clarke that the spirit convulsed him and probably meant to take his life but was not permitted. Calvin reads the amazement as a concession, the people compelled to acknowledge something more than man and rightly tracing the power of the miracle to the doctrine. Clarke ends on the word for the report, a very elegant metaphor of sound propagated by a stroke; Robertson notes that our word echo is in it, used of the roar of waves.
38:
Ambrose notices the pairing and gives a reason for its order: Luke having first shown a man delivered from an evil spirit goes on to a woman healed, because our Lord came to heal each sex, and he ought first to be healed who was first created. Bede observes that Christ cures sometimes at the request of others and sometimes unasked, which shows him far removed from the passions of sinners, always granting the prayer of the faithful, and either making intelligible what they do not understand in themselves or forgiving their not understanding it. Clarke draws a domestic moral instead — as soon as Peter began to follow Christ his family began to benefit, so that it is always profitable to contract an acquaintance with good men, one person full of faith and prayer drawing down blessings on his whole household. Robertson adds the flat historical note that Paul's reference to Peter's wife is pertinent here, and that the household lived together at Capernaum.

How the fever was removed produces a three-cornered disagreement. Origen says Luke speaks figuratively, as of a command given to a being capable of hearing it: the fever was commanded, and did not neglect the work of him who commanded. Calvin defends the same manner of speaking and explains it — to one not well acquainted with Scripture the expression may appear harsh, but diseases, famine, pestilence and calamities of every description are God's heralds, his bailiffs, by whom he executes his judgments, and as he sends them at his pleasure so he restrains and recalls them. Robertson denies the whole construction: we are surely not to take Luke to mean that Jesus took the exorcist's position and rebuked a malignant personality, since the attitude here is precisely that of any kindly and sympathetic physician, and where the other evangelists record the touch of her hand Luke gives the tender look over her head.

The crowd at sunset is explained by the calendar. Theophylact praises their zeal, bringing their sick after the sun had set and not deterred by the lateness of the day. Origen offers two reasons for the hour, either that they were employed about other things during the day or that they thought it unlawful to heal on the sabbath. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all give the second reason without the first, the sabbath being reckoned from sunset to sunset and ending just then, so that until that moment it would have been unlawful to bring the sick at all; Robertson adds the practical considerations, that it was cooler, that carrying a sick person was no longer counted work, and that by then the news of the two cures had spread over the whole town.

On the confession of the demons the notes are short and pointed. Robertson observes that thou art the Son of God is a more definite statement of the deity of Jesus than the demoniac's words in the synagogue, and enters the complaint that the word rendered devils ought always to be rendered demons. Gill notes that they came out unwillingly and not of themselves, but at the word and command of Christ. Cyril of Jerusalem, for once exactly on the text, sets the two receptions side by side: this Christ, when he was come, the Jews denied, but the devils confessed — and he adds that his forefather David was not ignorant of him, having ordained a lamp for his Anointed.
42:
Why he left a town that wanted him is answered first by Chrysostom, and answered in terms of the miracles themselves: when he had bestowed favour enough on the people by them it was necessary for him to depart, since miracles are always thought greater once the worker is gone, being then the more heeded and having, in their turn, a voice of their own. He adds the divided reception behind the departure — the Pharisees, seeing that the miracles published his fame, were offended at his power, while the people, hearing his words, assented and followed.

The crowd's pursuit is a matter of text and of tense. Clarke prefers the stronger reading of the verb, earnestly sought rather than simply sought, notes that it is supported by a long list of manuscripts and has been received into the text by two editors, and reads the eagerness as evidence that the people had tasted the good word of God and now clave to Christ with their whole heart; the word for detaining him, he adds, means that they caught hold of him. Robertson keeps to the narrative and fills it from the other Gospel, where it was a great while before day when Jesus rose — after a restless night, he supposes, following the excitement of the sabbath — and went out to pray; and he makes the pursuit a continuing action that succeeded, the multitudes keeping at it until they came right up to him. Gill notes only that they came the day after.

What Christ says he must do is then weighed word by word. Ellicott corrects the English: the verb is literally to evangelise and is quite distinct from the one commonly rendered preach, so that the sense is I must declare the glad tidings of the kingdom; and the object is not vaguely other cities but the other cities, with special reference to those of Galilee. Robertson reads the same clause as a refusal of favouritism — the urge was to go to all the cities and not to a favoured few — and observes that the reason given, for therefore was I sent, has a Johannine ring, Christ being the great Apostle of God to men. Clarke draws the consequence for the miracles: to proclaim the kingdom was the Messiah's great work, and the healing of diseases only an emblematical and secondary work, the proof of his goodness and the demonstration of his authority to preach — which sets the two in an order the reverse of the one Chrysostom had used to explain the departure.

On the closing summary the notes are brief. Gill takes it of the several synagogues in the different cities and towns throughout all Galilee; Ellicott and Robertson both make the verb a continuous imperfect, Robertson taking the verse as a description of the first tour of Galilee, whose details must be filled in from the other Gospels.
